newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia lawmakers take teeth out of anti-drug law.
newsitem.headline: Colombia lawmakers take teeth out of anti-drug law.

text.p: Colombian lawmakers have handed President Ernesto Samper a major setback by watering down a key provision of a bill designed to give the government powers to seize the assets of drug lords and their accomplices.

The government -- under strong U.S. pressure to crack down on Colombia's powerful cartels -- had asked that the so-called asset forfeiture law empower it to seize drug-related assets accumulated over the past 20 years.

The Senate approved the 20-year time limit in a vote last week. But the House of Representatives defeated it by 59-57 late on Tuesday, ruling instead that criminal assets would only be liable to forfeiture if they were acquired in the aftermath of the country's 1991 constitution.

The vote came despite impassioned pleas for support of the legislation from Samper and other top government officials, who argued that the international community would never understand it if lawmakers chose, in effect, to legalize profits from the drug trade.

Interior Minister Horacio Serpa, in a speech shortly before the vote, said any move to weaken the draft law would be totally self-destructive or "cannibalistic" since it would underscore the idea that Colombia -- where 99 percent of all crimes go unpunished -- is completely lawless and corrupt.

More importantly, perhaps, Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia said she had no doubt that Colombia, the world's top producer of cocaine and a leading supplier of heroin to the United States, would be hit with punitive U.S. economic sanctions if the law failed to win approval in the House.

The United States has threatened Colombia with sanctions ever since last March when Washington -- citing Samper's alleged ties to drug lords -- rendered the country a pariah state by including it on a list of countries that have failed to cooperate in the global anti-drug fight.

Samper lamented the vote in the lower house of Congress in a statement issued early Wednesday, saying that "without full retroactive powers" the asset forfeiture law was "an insufficient tool to effectively carry out our struggle against drug trafficking and organized crime."

Samper said he trusted that the 20-year time limit would restored, however, when the law is submitted to a conference committee to iron out the differences between the way it was passed in the Senate and the House.

The law, as drafted by the government in July, would allow the authorities to seize hundreds of millions of dollars in real estate holdings in Colombia, where up to 25 percent of all farm land is believed to be in the hands of traffickers, according to official figures.

Estimates vary as to how much money could be turned over to the state but some traffickers, including the jailed leaders of the Cali cartel, are said to have amassed personal fortunes totaling up to $12 billion.

In addition to asset forfeiture, the government has proposed stiffer prison sentences for drug kingpins as part of its U.S.-backed crackdown on the narcotics trade. Lawmakers took much of the teeth out of the sentencing law last week, however, by rejecting a call for mandatory terms totaling up to 30 years for anyone convicted of leading a criminal enterprise.

Legislators moved to soften the sentencing law further this week by proposing that congressmen jailed on drug-corruption charges should be entitled to house arrest instead of lowly prison cells. Several congressmen are already under arrest on drug charges and many are under suspicion of corruption or conspiring with drug lords.

The opposition Conservative Party has boycotted most sessions of Congress since last week and Tuesday's vote, which was deplored by crusading anti-drug prosecutor Alfonso Valdivieso, was almost entirely due to members of the ruling Liberal Party.
